topic: Broker Supervision of Salespersons & Associate Brokers
question: Under 19 NYCRR Section 175.21, the supervision a licensed broker must provide over a real estate salesperson is defined as consisting of:
choice_a: Regular, frequent, and consistent personal guidance, instruction, oversight, and superintendence with respect to the general real estate brokerage business
choice_b: A single orientation meeting at the time the salesperson is hired, with no ongoing obligation afterward
choice_c: Whatever level of oversight the broker personally deems convenient, with no defined regulatory standard
choice_d: Supervision only during the salesperson's first 90 days of association with the office
explanation: 19 NYCRR Section 175.21 defines a broker's supervisory duty over a salesperson as regular, frequent, and consistent personal guidance, instruction, oversight, and superintendence regarding the general real estate brokerage business and all related matters -- an ongoing obligation, not a one-time event.
source_note: 19 NYCRR Section 175.21 (Supervision of salesman by broker)

topic: Broker Supervision of Salespersons & Associate Brokers
question: Under 19 NYCRR Section 175.21, who is required to keep written records of listings obtained by a salesperson and of sales or other transactions effected with that salesperson's assistance?
choice_a: Only the salesperson, since the broker is not directly involved in each transaction
choice_b: Both the broker and the salesperson
choice_c: Only DOS, which maintains its own separate transaction log
choice_d: Only the buyer's attorney handling the closing
explanation: 19 NYCRR Section 175.21 places the recordkeeping duty on both the broker and the salesperson -- written records of listings and transactions effected during the salesperson's association with the office, sufficient to clearly identify the transactions and their dates.
source_note: 19 NYCRR Section 175.21 (Supervision of salesman by broker)

topic: Broker Supervision of Salespersons & Associate Brokers
question: What must the transaction records kept under Section 175.21 be sufficient to do?
choice_a: Include only the buyer's and seller's Social Security numbers
choice_b: Contain nothing more than the property's tax map number
choice_c: Clearly identify the transactions and indicate the dates on which they occurred
choice_d: Be limited exclusively to transactions that closed successfully, excluding any that fell through
explanation: Section 175.21 requires that the required listing/transaction records be sufficient to clearly identify each transaction and show the relevant dates -- supporting DOS's ability to verify supervision and experience claims.
source_note: 19 NYCRR Section 175.21 (Supervision of salesman by broker)

topic: Broker Supervision of Salespersons & Associate Brokers
question: A brokerage designates an associate broker to manage day-to-day operations and supervise the salespersons at one of its branch office locations. This associate broker is commonly referred to as the:
choice_a: Designated sales agent
choice_b: Escrow officer of record
choice_c: Nonresident co-broker
choice_d: Associate broker in charge of the branch office
explanation: New York brokerages commonly designate an associate broker in charge of a branch office to carry out the day-to-day supervisory duties over that office's salespersons and associate brokers, consistent with the broker's overall supervisory obligation under RPL Article 12-A and 19 NYCRR Part 175.
source_note: RPL Article 12-A; 19 NYCRR Sections 175.20-175.21 (branch office supervision practice)

topic: Broker Supervision of Salespersons & Associate Brokers
question: A real estate salesperson may lawfully engage in the general real estate brokerage business only:
choice_a: Under the supervision of a licensed real estate broker with whom the salesperson is associated
choice_b: Independently, once the salesperson has more than two years of experience
choice_c: Independently, as long as the salesperson maintains their own escrow account
choice_d: Under the supervision of any licensed attorney, whether or not that attorney is also a broker
explanation: A salesperson license is, by definition, dependent on association with and supervision by a licensed broker; a salesperson (regardless of years of experience) cannot practice independently of a supervising broker and cannot hold escrow funds directly.
source_note: RPL Article 12-A, Section 440 (definitions); 19 NYCRR Section 175.21

topic: Broker Supervision of Salespersons & Associate Brokers
question: If a broker classifies its salespersons as independent contractors for federal tax purposes, how does this affect the broker's supervisory and license-law responsibility for those salespersons' conduct?
choice_a: It completely eliminates the broker's supervisory duty, since independent contractors are legally autonomous
choice_b: It does not eliminate the broker's supervisory and license-law responsibility -- the broker remains accountable under RPL Article 12-A and Part 175 regardless of the salesperson's tax classification
choice_c: It shifts all disciplinary exposure for the salesperson's license law violations to DOS itself
choice_d: It automatically converts the salesperson into an associate broker
explanation: Federal independent-contractor tax status (relevant to compensation and withholding) is a separate question from license-law supervisory responsibility -- New York's broker-supervision framework holds the broker accountable for oversight of its associated salespersons' real estate activity regardless of that tax classification, a principle sometimes summarized in practice guidance as 'let the broker beware.'
source_note: RPL Article 12-A; 19 NYCRR Section 175.21 (broker supervisory accountability distinct from federal tax classification)

topic: Broker Supervision of Salespersons & Associate Brokers
question: A DOS investigation finds that a salesperson repeatedly violated fair housing law over several transactions, and that the supervising broker took no steps to monitor, train, or correct the salesperson's conduct. What is a realistic regulatory consequence for the broker?
choice_a: The broker faces no exposure, because only the individual salesperson who committed the violations can be disciplined
choice_b: The broker's license is automatically revoked with no hearing or opportunity to respond
choice_c: The broker can face independent discipline for failing to provide adequate supervision, separate from any discipline imposed on the salesperson directly
choice_d: DOS may only issue a warning letter to the brokerage's landlord
explanation: New York's broker-supervision framework -- reinforced by amendments strengthening broker accountability for housing discrimination by associated licensees -- exposes a broker to independent discipline for failing to provide the regular, frequent supervision required by Section 175.21, separate from any action against the individual salesperson.
source_note: 19 NYCRR Section 175.21; RPL Article 12-A discipline provisions; NY fair housing supervisory-duty amendments (well-corroborated industry legal commentary)

topic: Broker Supervision of Salespersons & Associate Brokers
question: Under 19 NYCRR Section 175.25, a real estate 'team' is defined as:
choice_a: Any group of five or more licensees working in the same physical office
choice_b: A brokerage's entire sales staff, regardless of how they market themselves
choice_c: Only unlicensed marketing assistants who support a single agent
choice_d: Two or more persons, at least one of whom is an associate real estate broker or real estate salesperson associated with the same brokerage, who hold themselves out or operate as a team
explanation: 19 NYCRR Section 175.25 defines a 'team' for advertising-regulation purposes as two or more persons -- at least one an associate broker or salesperson associated with the same brokerage -- who hold themselves out or operate as a team.
source_note: 19 NYCRR Section 175.25 (Advertising -- team definition)

topic: Broker Supervision of Salespersons & Associate Brokers
question: Under the team-advertising rule, what word must appear in a team's marketing name?
choice_a: The word 'team' itself
choice_b: The word 'associates'
choice_c: The word 'group'
choice_d: The word 'realty'
explanation: 19 NYCRR Section 175.25 requires that a team's name use the term 'team' -- terms such as 'associates,' 'realty,' or 'group' are specifically prohibited as substitutes, to avoid public confusion with a licensed brokerage entity.
source_note: 19 NYCRR Section 175.25 (Advertising -- team name requirements)

topic: Broker Supervision of Salespersons & Associate Brokers
question: A team markets itself simply as 'The Summit Group' without including any individual licensee's name. Under 19 NYCRR Section 175.25, what must follow the team name?
choice_a: Nothing further is required as long as a phone number is listed
choice_b: The word 'at' or 'of' followed by the name of the brokerage with which the team is associated
choice_c: The names of every past client the team has represented
choice_d: A disclaimer that the team is not affiliated with any brokerage
explanation: If a team name does not include the full licensed names of the team's members, Section 175.25 requires the team name be immediately followed by 'at' or 'of' plus the associated brokerage's name, so the public can identify the licensed firm behind the team.
source_note: 19 NYCRR Section 175.25 (Advertising -- team name disclosure)

topic: Broker Supervision of Salespersons & Associate Brokers
question: May a team's marketing name include the name of an unlicensed individual (e.g., an unlicensed marketing coordinator)?
choice_a: Yes, without any restriction
choice_b: Yes, but only if that person is the broker's spouse
choice_c: No -- the use of an unlicensed individual's name in a team name is prohibited
choice_d: Yes, as long as the unlicensed person pays a fee to DOS
explanation: 19 NYCRR Section 175.25 prohibits including an unlicensed individual's name within the team's marketing name itself, to prevent the public from mistakenly believing an unlicensed person holds broker or salesperson authority.
source_note: 19 NYCRR Section 175.25 (Advertising -- unlicensed individuals)

topic: Broker Supervision of Salespersons & Associate Brokers
question: If a team's advertisement separately references unlicensed support staff by name (outside the team name itself), what does Section 175.25 require?
choice_a: No disclosure is required as long as the unlicensed staff member does not negotiate offers
choice_b: The unlicensed staff member's name must be printed in a font at least as large as the broker's name
choice_c: Unlicensed staff may never be mentioned anywhere in any advertisement
choice_d: The advertisement must clearly and conspicuously state which individuals are licensees and which are not
explanation: Where an advertisement names unlicensed individuals associated with a team, 19 NYCRR Section 175.25 requires the ad to clearly and conspicuously identify which named individuals are licensed real estate professionals and which are not, preventing public confusion about who is legally authorized to perform brokerage activity.
source_note: 19 NYCRR Section 175.25 (Advertising -- disclosure of unlicensed individuals)

topic: Broker Supervision of Salespersons & Associate Brokers
question: Why does New York regulate team names and require brokerage identification within them, even though the individual team members are already licensed?
choice_a: Because a team name that omits the sponsoring brokerage could mislead the public into thinking the team operates as its own independent licensed entity
choice_b: Because DOS charges an extra licensing fee for every team name
choice_c: Because teams are legally required to be separately incorporated from their brokerage
choice_d: Because team advertising is entirely unregulated apart from this one naming rule
explanation: The team-naming rules in Section 175.25 exist to prevent public confusion -- ensuring consumers can identify both the licensed individuals and the licensed brokerage actually responsible for and supervising the team's activity.
source_note: 19 NYCRR Section 175.25 (Advertising -- purpose of team disclosure rules)

topic: Broker Supervision of Salespersons & Associate Brokers
question: A newly licensed salesperson asks whether they may accept a referral fee directly from a title company without informing their broker. Under New York's supervisory framework, is this permitted?
choice_a: Yes, as long as the fee is under $100
choice_b: No -- a salesperson may not accept compensation related to real estate activity from anyone other than their supervising broker without the broker's knowledge and involvement
choice_c: Yes, referral fees are entirely outside the scope of broker supervision
choice_d: Yes, provided the title company is not a party to the transaction
explanation: Consistent with RPL Section 442-a (a salesperson may be compensated only by their supervising broker) and the broker's overall supervisory duty, a salesperson accepting outside compensation without the broker's knowledge undermines both the compensation rule and the broker's ability to supervise the salesperson's real estate-related activity.
source_note: RPL Article 12-A, Section 442-a; 19 NYCRR Section 175.21 (supervisory oversight of compensation-related conduct)

topic: Broker Supervision of Salespersons & Associate Brokers
question: A broker delegates day-to-day supervisory duties for a branch office to an associate broker in charge, but never visits the branch, reviews its files, or communicates with that associate broker about office practices. Does delegation alone satisfy the broker's supervisory obligation?
choice_a: Yes -- once supervisory duties are delegated to any associate broker, the licensed broker has no further obligation whatsoever
choice_b: Yes -- delegation is only relevant for escrow accounts, not for salesperson supervision
choice_c: No -- Section 175.21's standard of regular, frequent, and consistent oversight applies to the overall supervisory structure, and mere delegation without any ongoing engagement is unlikely to satisfy it
choice_d: No -- delegation of supervisory duties to an associate broker is never permitted under any circumstance
explanation: While a broker may appoint an associate broker in charge of a branch to help carry out supervisory duties, the regulatory standard under 175.21 -- regular, frequent, consistent personal guidance and oversight -- is not satisfied by pure delegation with zero ongoing engagement; DOS can still hold the broker of record accountable for supervisory failures.
source_note: 19 NYCRR Section 175.21 (Supervision of salesman by broker)

topic: Broker Supervision of Salespersons & Associate Brokers
question: Which of the following is an accurate statement about associate brokers and their supervisory relationship to the sponsoring broker?
choice_a: An associate broker is entirely exempt from any broker's supervision because they already hold broker-level qualifications
choice_b: An associate broker automatically becomes the broker of record for any office they work in
choice_c: An associate broker may independently maintain an escrow account separate from the sponsoring broker's account
choice_d: An associate broker, though qualified to hold an independent broker license, still operates under the sponsoring broker's license and supervision while associated with that broker's office
explanation: Even though an associate broker has met all broker-level qualification requirements, while associated with a brokerage they remain under that broker's license and supervisory structure -- they do not independently hold escrow authority or automatically become the broker of record.
source_note: RPL Article 12-A, Section 440 (definitions -- associate broker); 19 NYCRR Part 175

topic: Broker Supervision of Salespersons & Associate Brokers
question: What is the primary regulatory purpose behind requiring brokers and salespersons to jointly maintain written listing and transaction records under Section 175.21?
choice_a: To create a verifiable trail supporting supervision, experience credit, and DOS's ability to investigate complaints or license-renewal claims
choice_b: To help brokers calculate their annual property tax liability
choice_c: To satisfy IRS Form 1099 reporting requirements exclusively
choice_d: To provide marketing material for the brokerage's website
explanation: The written listing/transaction recordkeeping duty under Section 175.21 supports DOS's ability to verify a broker's supervisory practices, confirm a salesperson's claimed experience (relevant to future broker-license applications), and investigate complaints -- not tax or marketing purposes.
source_note: 19 NYCRR Section 175.21 (Supervision of salesman by broker)

topic: Broker Supervision of Salespersons & Associate Brokers
question: A broker's office has salespersons working from home and communicating with the broker only sporadically over several months, with no file review, meetings, or check-ins. From a license-law compliance standpoint, this arrangement is:
choice_a: Fully compliant, because remote work eliminates any in-person supervision requirement
choice_b: A likely violation of the Section 175.21 supervision standard, which calls for regular, frequent, and consistent oversight regardless of where the salesperson physically works
choice_c: Irrelevant to license law, which only regulates where escrow funds are kept
choice_d: Compliant as long as the salesperson has more than five years of experience
explanation: Section 175.21's supervisory standard is not satisfied merely by physical proximity or its absence -- what matters is the regularity, frequency, and consistency of the broker's actual guidance and oversight, which sporadic, months-apart contact does not meet.
source_note: 19 NYCRR Section 175.21 (Supervision of salesman by broker)

topic: Broker Supervision of Salespersons & Associate Brokers
question: A salesperson signs a listing agreement using only their own name and phone number, with no reference anywhere to their supervising brokerage. Is this compliant with New York's licensing and advertising framework?
choice_a: Yes -- salespersons may contract independently of their broker once they have signed at least one prior listing
choice_b: Yes -- only teams, not individual salespersons, must reference their brokerage
choice_c: No -- a salesperson's real estate activity, including listing agreements and advertising, must be conducted in association with and under the name/authority of their supervising broker
choice_d: Yes -- this is permitted as long as the client is a personal friend of the salesperson
explanation: A salesperson has no independent authority to contract for brokerage services -- all listing agreements and related activity must be conducted under, and identify, the supervising broker, consistent with the salesperson's dependent licensure status under RPL Article 12-A.
source_note: RPL Article 12-A, Section 440 (definitions); 19 NYCRR Section 175.21

topic: Broker Supervision of Salespersons & Associate Brokers
question: Which best describes the overall relationship between a broker's supervisory duty under Section 175.21 and the broker's exposure to DOS discipline for a salesperson's misconduct?
choice_a: The broker's supervisory conduct is entirely irrelevant to any DOS disciplinary proceeding
choice_b: Only the salesperson who committed misconduct can ever be disciplined by DOS
choice_c: Supervision only matters for escrow-related misconduct, not for other license law violations
choice_d: Adequate documented supervision helps demonstrate the broker met its regulatory obligations, while a documented failure to supervise can expose the broker to independent discipline even where the salesperson acted alone
explanation: Because Section 175.21 imposes an affirmative, ongoing supervisory duty on the broker, the adequacy (or inadequacy) of that supervision is directly relevant to DOS discipline -- a broker who can show regular, frequent, documented oversight is in a materially different position than one who cannot.
source_note: 19 NYCRR Section 175.21; RPL Article 12-A discipline provisions

topic: Broker Supervision of Salespersons & Associate Brokers
question: A team advertisement lists the team as 'Premier Associates' without any reference to a licensed brokerage or the word 'team.' Which rule(s) does this most likely violate?
choice_a: It violates both the requirement to use the word 'team' in the name and the requirement to identify the sponsoring brokerage
choice_b: It violates no rule, since 'Associates' is an acceptable synonym for 'team'
choice_c: It only violates a rule if the team has fewer than two members
choice_d: It is compliant as long as a business card lists the brokerage separately
explanation: 19 NYCRR Section 175.25 requires the word 'team' (not substitutes like 'associates') in a team's marketing name, and requires either the members' full licensed names or the brokerage's name (via 'at/of') to appear -- 'Premier Associates' standing alone fails both requirements.
source_note: 19 NYCRR Section 175.25 (Advertising -- team name requirements)

topic: Broker Supervision of Salespersons & Associate Brokers
question: In New York, which license type is legally barred from independently maintaining a client trust/escrow account, regardless of years of experience?
choice_a: Only unlicensed office administrators
choice_b: Real estate salespersons and associate brokers
choice_c: Only brokers who have not completed continuing education
choice_d: No license type is barred from maintaining escrow accounts
explanation: Only the licensed broker (the broker of record) may maintain the brokerage's escrow account; salespersons and associate brokers -- even highly experienced ones -- are barred from independently holding client trust funds, reinforcing the broker's central supervisory and fiduciary role.
source_note: RPL Article 12-A; 19 NYCRR Section 175.1 (broker-exclusive escrow authority)

topic: Broker Supervision of Salespersons & Associate Brokers
question: Why is broker-level supervision considered a cornerstone of New York's real estate licensing scheme rather than a purely administrative formality?
choice_a: Because it exists solely to help brokers collect a larger share of commission splits
choice_b: Because DOS requires it only for brokerages with more than 50 licensees
choice_c: Because it is the mechanism by which the license law ensures consumer protection, trust-fund safety, and legal compliance are maintained across every transaction a salesperson handles
choice_d: Because it applies only during a salesperson's probationary first year
explanation: Broker supervision is structurally central to New York's license law: it is the regulatory lever ensuring that consumer protections, trust-account integrity, agency disclosure, fair housing compliance, and general legal conduct are maintained at the level of every individual transaction a salesperson conducts.
source_note: RPL Article 12-A; 19 NYCRR Part 175 (broker-centered regulatory design)
